claims.text: The untreated (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy exhibits a strong caloric response under applied magnetic and pressure fields.
The untreated alloy has poor load-bearing integrity and tends to crack.
Room-temperature high-pressure torsion at several gigapascals for a controlled number of rotations will produce a nanostructured, ultrafine-grained state.
High-pressure torsion will significantly refine the alloy's grain size.
High-pressure torsion will create stronger, more coherent grain boundaries.
The refined grain structure and strengthened grain boundaries will suppress crack initiation and propagation.
The increased density of grain boundaries produced by high-pressure torsion will act as barriers to crack propagation and thereby enhance toughness.
Controlled high-pressure torsion will not introduce a secondary phase that interferes with the reversible caloric phase transition.
Controlled high-pressure torsion will not substantially alter the alloy's bulk phase composition.
Controlled high-pressure torsion will leave the energetics of the martensitic or similar caloric transformation substantially unchanged.
The transformation responsible for the caloric effect is sensitive to alloy chemistry and lattice parameters.
The transformation will remain robust if deformation is controlled to avoid excessive damage.
High-pressure torsion will increase fracture toughness by an estimated 30–50% relative to the untreated alloy.
High-pressure-torsion-treated samples will retain a caloric-response magnitude similar to that of the untreated alloy under magnetic and pressure fields.
High-pressure-torsion-treated samples will retain caloric reversibility similar to that of the untreated alloy under magnetic and pressure fields.
The intervention is expected to remain valid when processing is performed near room temperature and below temperatures that activate or alter the phase transformation.
The intervention is expected to remain valid only within field and pressure ranges that do not exceed the alloy's caloric-cycle limits.
Excessive deformation could shift transformation parameters or reduce the caloric effect.
